steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an NLP paper proposing a multi-bit watermark for large language models, so that machine-generated text can be traced back to the user who produced it rather than only identified. Motivate the need beyond detection, explain the shortcomings of existing multi-bit methods, and summarize our method and headline result.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Opening: beyond identifying machine-generated text; LLM popularity and misuse; detection methods
- Higher-stakes misuse and the need to trace the adversary user
- Existing multi-bit watermarking and its limitations
- Our method (MPAC) and main result

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Opening
  - question: how to go further than identifying machine-generated text, to proactively tackle LLM misuse?
  - human-like LMs, accessible via web interface and APIs -> unprecedented public and academic attention
  - following complex instructions boosts productivity: programming, creative writing
  - concerns: automating malicious activities like spreading disinformation
  - detection methods: zero-shot detection, supervised training, watermarking
  - identifying machine-generated content = pivotal step against harm
- Higher stakes
  - misinformation and war propaganda on social media for political or financial gains; erosion of social trust
  - identifying text may not suffice for LM providers; need to trace back to adversary user
  - API providers can ban users; media/social platforms + API providers collaborate with law enforcement
  - watermarking user information (or part) holds adversary accountable without storing user queries (prohibitively expensive, privacy concern)
- Existing multi-bit methods
  - achieved by embedding multi-bit information
  - recent works: distinct signal for each multi-bit message
  - fine at low bit-width, low noise; harder as bit-width grows (exponential number of messages); worse with higher noise
  - considering all messages -> increased latency in encoding and/or decoding; encoding latency degrades user experience
- Our method: Multi-bit watermark via Position Allocation (MPAC) (Fig. 1)
  - pseudo-randomly allocate each token to a sub-unit of the message
  - longer messages without added generation latency; fares well under high corruption
  - message content at allocated position decides state to encode with a zero-bit scheme (e.g. which token subsets are biased)
  - more load capacity: partition vocabulary into multiple "colored" lists instead of one green list -> multiple states per token
  - result: robustness improves over runner-up baseline by \geq 20% in high-noise setting for 16-bit and 24-bit messages

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
How can we go further than just identifying machine-generated text and actually tackle misuses of large language models proactively? Language models are now human-like and easy to access through web interfaces and APIs, and so they have gotten unprecedented attention from the public and from academia. Because they can follow complex instructions, they have boosted productivity on many tasks such as programming, creative writing, and more. But there are growing concerns that such language models will be exploited to automate malicious activities like spreading disinformation. Because of this, various methods have been developed to detect machine-generated texts, using techniques such as zero-shot detection, supervised training, watermarking, and more. These efforts are focused on identifying machine-generated content, which is an important step for reducing the potential harm of such text.

But for more pernicious misuses of large language models, such as spreading misinformation and war propaganda on social media platforms for political or financial gains, the stakes are much higher, and this could lead to the erosion of social trust. In these cases just identifying the machine-generated text may not be enough for the language model providers. What becomes important instead is being able to trace back to the adversary user who generated the content, so such misuses can be counteracted. Then the API providers can take a precursory measure and ban these users from their systems, and media and social platforms together with API providers can work with law enforcement authorities and take more decisive actions. Overall, watermarking the user information (or part of it) can hold the adversary user accountable for harms done through language model APIs without having to store user queries, which would be prohibitively expensive and would worry ordinary users who care about privacy.

- Existing multi-bit methods
  - embed multi-bit information; recent works give a distinct signal per message
  - ok for low bit-width / low noise; harder as bit-width grows (exponential messages); worse with noise
  - all messages considered -> latency in encoding/decoding; encoding latency hurts user experience
- Our method: Multi-bit watermark via Position Allocation (MPAC) (Fig. 1)
  - pseudo-random allocation of tokens to message sub-units; long messages, no added latency, robust to corruption
  - message content at position picks state for zero-bit scheme (which token subsets biased)
  - multiple "colored" lists instead of single green list -> more load capacity
  - \geq 20% robustness over runner-up baseline, high noise, 16-bit and 24-bit

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
How can we go further than just identifying machine-generated text and actually tackle misuses of large language models proactively? Language models are now human-like and easy to access through web interfaces and APIs, and so they have gotten unprecedented attention from the public and from academia. Because they can follow complex instructions, they have boosted productivity on many tasks such as programming, creative writing, and more. But there are growing concerns that such language models will be exploited to automate malicious activities like spreading disinformation. Because of this, various methods have been developed to detect machine-generated texts, using techniques such as zero-shot detection, supervised training, watermarking, and more. These efforts are focused on identifying machine-generated content, which is an important step for reducing the potential harm of such text.

But for more pernicious misuses of large language models, such as spreading misinformation and war propaganda on social media platforms for political or financial gains, the stakes are much higher, and this could lead to the erosion of social trust. In these cases just identifying the machine-generated text may not be enough for the language model providers. What becomes important instead is being able to trace back to the adversary user who generated the content, so such misuses can be counteracted. Then the API providers can take a precursory measure and ban these users from their systems, and media and social platforms together with API providers can work with law enforcement authorities and take more decisive actions. Overall, watermarking the user information (or part of it) can hold the adversary user accountable for harms done through language model APIs without having to store user queries, which would be prohibitively expensive and would worry ordinary users who care about privacy.

All of this can be done by embedding multi-bit information. Recent works do this by giving a distinct signal for each multi-bit message. This works in low bit-width and low noise settings, but it gets harder and harder to keep the watermark intact as the bit-width increases, because the number of possible messages is exponential. This gets worse when there is higher noise. Also, having to consider all the possible messages has the side effect of more latency in the encoding and/or decoding phase, and latency in encoding makes the end user experience worse.

Our proposed method, Multi-bit watermark via Position Allocation (MPAC), is different. It first allocates each token pseudo-randomly onto a sub-unit of the message to be embedded (Fig. 1). Because the tokens are allocated onto different parts of the message, longer messages can be embedded without added generation latency, and it does well in high corruption settings. Then the message content at the allocated position decides the state to encode with a zero-bit watermarking scheme. For example, if we follow an existing zero-bit watermarking scheme, the message content decides which token subsets are biased. To increase load capacity we can also partition the vocabulary into multiple "colored" lists instead of one green list, which encodes multiple states for every token. In our experiments our method improves the robustness of the watermark over the runner-up baseline by \geq 20% in the high-noise setting for 16-bit and 24-bit messages.

steps.text:

But for more pernicious misuses of large language models, such as spreading misinformation and war propaganda on social media platforms for political or financial gains [6,7,8], the stakes are much higher, and this could lead to the erosion of social trust [9]. In these cases just identifying the machine-generated text may not be enough for the language model providers. What becomes important instead is being able to trace back to the adversary user who generated the content, so such misuses can be counteracted. Then the API providers can take a precursory measure and ban these users from their systems, and media and social platforms together with API providers can work with law enforcement authorities and take more decisive actions. All of this can be done by embedding multi-bit information. Recent works [10,11] do this by giving a distinct signal for each multi-bit message. This works in low bit-width and low noise settings, but it gets harder and harder to keep the watermark intact as the bit-width increases, because the number of possible messages is exponential. This gets worse when there is higher noise. Also, having to consider all the possible messages has the side effect of more latency in the encoding and/or decoding phase, and latency in encoding makes the end user experience worse.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
How can we take a step further from merely identifying machine-generated text to proactively tackling misuses of large language models? The emergence of human-like language models and their easy accessibility via web interface and APIs have attracted unprecedented attention from the public and academia [1]. The ability to follow complex instructions has boosted the productivity of various tasks such as programming, creative writing, and more. However, there have been growing concerns about exploiting such language models to automate malicious activities such as spreading disinformation. This has led to the development of various methods to detect machine-generated texts through techniques such as zero-shot detection, supervised training, watermarking, and more [2,3,4,5]. These efforts focus on the crucial task of identifying machine-generated content, which is a pivotal step in mitigating the potential harm caused by such text.

However, when it comes to more pernicious misuses of large language models, such as the dissemination of misinformation and war propaganda on social media platforms for political or financial gains [6,7,8], the stakes are considerably higher, potentially leading to the erosion of social trust [9]. In such circumstances, merely identifying the machine-generated text may not be enough for the language model providers. Instead, the ability to trace back to the adversary user responsible for generating the content becomes pivotal in counteracting such misuses. In this way, the API providers can take a precursory measure to ban these users from their systems and allow media and social platforms, along with API providers, to collaborate with law enforcement authorities and take more decisive actions. All in all, watermarking the user information (or part thereof) can hold the adversary user accountable for potential harms facilitated through language model APIs without having to store user queries [5], which would be prohibitively expensive and concern ordinary users who value privacy.

All this can be achieved by embedding multi-bit information. Recent works [10,11] achieve this by providing a distinct signal for each multi-bit message. While this is effective in low bit-width and low noise settings, maintaining the integrity of the watermark becomes increasingly difficult as the bit-width increases due to the exponential number of possible messages. This is made worse in the presence of higher noise. In addition, having to consider all the possible messages comes with the side effect of increased latency during the encoding and/or decoding phase, the former of which degrades the end user experience.

In contrast, our proposed method Multi-bit watermark via Position Allocation (MPAC) first allocates each token pseudo-randomly onto a sub-unit of the message to be embedded (Fig. 1). Allocating tokens onto different parts of the message allows the embedding of longer messages without added generation latency and fares well in high corruption settings. Then the message content at the allocated position determines the state to encode using a zero-bit watermarking scheme. For instance, when following the zero-bit watermarking scheme of [4], the message content decides which token subsets are biased. To increase load capacity, we can further partition the vocabulary into multiple "colored" lists instead of a single green list, effectively encoding multiple states for every token. Our experiments show that our method improves upon the runner-up baseline in terms of watermark robustness by \geq 20% in the high-noise setting for 16-bit and 24-bit messages.
